subject: critical_thinking
subtopic: Identifying a necessary assumption: validity of a proxy measure (the observed indicator must reflect the target quantity)
learning_objective: Identify the unstated assumption that a measured indicator validly reflects the underlying quantity a conclusion is about (proxy validity), and confirm it with the negation test.
question:
A university wants to raise the quality of its undergraduate teaching. It introduces a scheme that pays each lecturer an annual bonus based on the average satisfaction score that students award them in end-of-course questionnaires. Two years later, average student-satisfaction scores have risen substantially. The Vice-Chancellor concludes that the quality of the university's teaching has improved.

Which of the following is an assumption on which the Vice-Chancellor's conclusion depends?

choices.A: Financial incentives are the most effective available means of improving teaching quality.
choices.B: The rise in satisfaction scores reflects a genuine improvement in teaching rather than changes lecturers made that raised their scores without improving their teaching.
choices.C: Every lecturer received a larger bonus in the second year than in the first year.
choices.D: Before the scheme was introduced, lecturers had no incentive of any kind to teach well.
choices.E: If the bonus scheme had not been introduced, average satisfaction scores would not have risen.

explanation: The argument moves from an observed rise in a measured indicator (student-satisfaction scores) to a conclusion about an unobserved target quantity (teaching quality). Whenever an argument leans on a proxy, it silently assumes the proxy is valid — that a change in the indicator reflects a change in the thing it stands for. The negation test isolates the necessary assumption: negate each option and check whether the conclusion still stands. Only negating B (the scores rose without any real improvement, e.g. through grade inflation or easier assessment) destroys the inference, so B is the assumption the conclusion depends on. The others are too strong (A, D), about what caused the rise rather than what it shows (C), or irrelevant detail (E).

option_analysis.A: Wrong: A comparative superlative ('most effective available means') is not required. The argument needs only that quality improved, not that this was the best possible method. Negating it does not undermine the conclusion. Misconception: over-reaching to a comparative claim the argument never makes.
option_analysis.B: Correct: The Vice-Chancellor uses the rise in satisfaction scores (a proxy) as evidence for a rise in teaching quality (the target). This step works only if higher scores actually track better teaching. Negation test: if the scores rose through means unrelated to teaching quality — grade inflation, easier assessments, more entertaining but thinner lectures — the conclusion collapses. So the argument depends on the proxy being valid.
option_analysis.C: Wrong: An administrative detail about individual bonus sizes is irrelevant to whether teaching quality improved; the argument relies on the average score, not on every individual's bonus increasing. Misconception: mistaking an incidental factual detail for a load-bearing assumption.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: This is far stronger than the argument needs. The conclusion only claims teaching improved after the scheme; it does not require there to have been zero prior incentives. Negating it (lecturers did have some prior incentive) leaves the conclusion intact. Misconception: treating an extreme, absolute claim as the needed assumption.
option_analysis.E: Wrong: This concerns whether the scheme caused the rise (a causal-attribution/counterfactual claim). The conclusion is about what the observed rise shows about teaching quality, not about what caused the scores to move. The scores did rise, as stated; the argument need not attribute that to the scheme. Misconception: confusing a proxy-validity assumption with a claim about causal attribution.

subject: critical_thinking
subtopic: Weakening a causal claim by regression to the mean (subjects selected on an extreme value drift toward the average regardless of any intervention)
learning_objective: Recognise that when subjects are selected because a fluctuating measurement was extreme, a later movement toward the average is expected without any intervention, and identify this regression-to-the-mean point as the strongest weakener of a causal claim.
question:
Last year, the ten hospitals in a region with the highest recorded rates of post-operative infection were required to adopt a new hand-hygiene protocol. This year, the average infection rate at those ten hospitals fell by 30%, a much larger fall than that seen across the region as a whole. A health official concludes that the new protocol is highly effective at reducing post-operative infections.

Which of the following, if true, most weakens the official's conclusion?

choices.A: Implementing the new protocol turned out to be more expensive than the hospitals had anticipated.
choices.B: No other changes to infection-control practice were made at the ten hospitals during the year.
choices.C: Post-operative infections are generally more common after emergency operations than after planned operations.
choices.D: The region as a whole also recorded a small fall in its average post-operative infection rate this year.
choices.E: The ten hospitals were selected precisely because their infection rates last year were exceptionally high, and each hospital's rate varies from year to year around a stable long-term average.

explanation: This is a selection-on-an-extreme setup: the hospitals entered the programme because they had the highest infection rates in a single year. When a fluctuating quantity is measured, an unusually high reading tends to be followed by a lower one simply because the extreme was partly due to chance — regression to the mean. That mechanism alone predicts the observed larger-than-average fall, so it is a genuine rival to the protocol explanation and is the strongest weakener (D). Distractor A is compatible with the argument (the ten still fell by more); B actually strengthens it by removing confounders; C is an irrelevant general fact; E addresses cost, not effectiveness. This weakening route is distinct from a simple confounder, a pre-existing downward trend, or reverse causation.

option_analysis.A: Wrong: Cost bears on whether the protocol is worthwhile, not on whether it actually reduced infections. It leaves the effectiveness claim untouched. Misconception: conflating cost-effectiveness with causal effectiveness.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: Ruling out other simultaneous changes removes rival explanations, which if anything strengthens the causal claim. Misconception: confusing eliminating a confounder (a strengthener) with weakening the argument.
option_analysis.C: Wrong: A general fact about which operations carry more infection risk is not tied to any change between the two years and gives no reason to doubt that the protocol caused the fall. Misconception: treating an irrelevant true statement as relevant because it is 'about' infections.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: This is consistent with the argument rather than damaging to it. The ten hospitals fell by more than the region, so a small region-wide fall does not explain their larger drop. Misconception: assuming any mention of a background change automatically undermines the claim.
option_analysis.E: Correct: The ten hospitals were chosen because their rates were at an extreme (the highest) in one year, and rates fluctuate around a stable average. Values selected because they are unusually high tend to fall back toward the average the next year even with no intervention — regression to the mean. This supplies a complete alternative explanation for the larger-than-average fall, directly undermining the claim that the protocol caused it.

subject: critical_thinking
subtopic: Tracking the top face of a die rolled (tipped) through a sequence of moves on a grid
learning_objective: Track the orientation of a cube as it is rolled over its edges through a sequence of moves, updating which face occupies each position, to determine the final uppermost face.
question:
A cube-shaped die rests on a square grid. Its opposite faces sum to 7 (so 1 is opposite 6, 2 is opposite 5, and 3 is opposite 4). At the start, the face showing 1 is on top, the face showing 2 faces South (toward you), and the face showing 3 faces East.

The die is now rolled — tipped over one edge at a time, without sliding — through the following sequence of moves: first one square East, then one square North, then one square East again.

Which number is on the top face of the die after these three moves?
explanation: Model the die by its six positions (top, bottom, north, south, east, west) and update them at each roll. A roll to the East cycles top to east, east to bottom, bottom to west, west to top, and leaves north and south fixed; a roll to the North cycles top to north, north to bottom, bottom to south, south to top, and leaves east and west fixed. From the start Top=1, South=2, East=3 (so Bottom=6, North=5, West=4): after East the top is 4; after North the top is 2; after the second East the top is 6. Keeping opposite faces paired (sum 7) is a useful check at every step. The distractors correspond to stopping early (2), reading the wrong position (3, 4), or losing orientation (5).

option_analysis.A: Wrong: 4 is the top face after just the first roll East (and it ends up facing North at the finish); it is neither the intermediate nor the final top after all three moves. Misconception: reading the top after a single move, or confusing the North face with the top.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: 3 is the number facing South at the end of the sequence, not the number on top. Misconception: tracking the wrong position (the front/South face instead of the top).
option_analysis.C: Correct: Rolling East sends top to east, east to bottom, bottom to west, west to top; rolling North sends top to north, north to bottom, bottom to south, south to top. Starting from Top=1, South=2, East=3 (so Bottom=6, North=5, West=4): after East the top is 4; after North the top is 2; after the second East the top is 6. The final top face shows 6.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: 5 is on the hidden bottom face after the first two rolls; the die then rolls East again. Misconception: losing track of orientation and reporting a side or bottom face.
option_analysis.E: Wrong: 2 is the top face after only the first two rolls (East, then North). It ignores the third roll (a second move East), which brings 6 to the top. Misconception: stopping the sequence one step early.

subject: critical_thinking
subtopic: Joint variation: direct with one factor and the square of a second, inverse with a third
learning_objective: Apply combined (joint) variation — direct proportionality to one quantity and to the square of another, and inverse proportionality to a third — by forming the correct ratio of scale factors and computing a new value.
question:
The maximum load L that a rectangular wooden beam can safely support varies directly with the beam's width w, directly with the square of its depth d, and inversely with its length l. A first beam has width 6 cm, depth 10 cm and length 3 m, and can safely support a load of 900 kg. A second beam of the same material has width 4 cm, depth 15 cm and length 5 m.

What maximum load can the second beam safely support?
explanation: Write the joint variation as L = k*w*d^2/l. Rather than find k, take the ratio of the two beams so k cancels: L2 = L1 * (w2/w1) * (d2/d1)^2 * (l1/l2). Substituting, L2 = 900 * (4/6) * (15/10)^2 * (3/5) = 900 * (2/3) * (9/4) * (3/5) = 810 kg. Two traps dominate: forgetting to square the depth ratio (gives 540) and using the length ratio the wrong way up — a longer beam must support less, so the factor is 3/5, not 5/3; the wrong way gives 2250.

option_analysis.A: Correct: L varies as w*d^2/l, so L2 = L1 * (w2/w1) * (d2/d1)^2 * (l1/l2) = 900 * (4/6) * (15/10)^2 * (3/5) = 900 * (2/3) * (9/4) * (3/5) = 810 kg. Note the length ratio is inverted (l1/l2) because the load is inversely proportional to length.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: 1350 kg omits the length factor altogether: 900 * (2/3) * (9/4). Because the second beam is longer (5 m vs 3 m), the inverse-length factor of 3/5 must reduce the load. Misconception: dropping the inverse-proportion term.
option_analysis.C: Wrong: 540 kg comes from using the depth to the first power, 900 * (4/6) * (15/10) * (3/5), omitting the square on the depth ratio. Misconception: ignoring the 'square of its depth' in the joint-variation relationship.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: 2250 kg treats length as directly proportional, using (5/3) instead of (3/5). Since L varies inversely with l, a longer beam supports less, not more. Misconception: inverting the direction of an inverse-proportion factor.
option_analysis.E: Wrong: 360 kg comes from squaring the width instead of the depth: 900 * (4/6)^2 * (15/10) * (3/5). The problem states L varies with the square of the depth, not the width. Misconception: attaching the square to the wrong variable.

subject: critical_thinking
subtopic: Matching the structure of a valid modus tollens argument across varied content (vs modus ponens, affirming the consequent, denying the antecedent, hypothetical syllogism)
learning_objective: Abstract the logical form of a valid modus tollens argument (if P then Q; not Q; therefore not P) and match it to another argument with different content, distinguishing it from modus ponens, affirming the consequent, denying the antecedent and a hypothetical syllogism.
question:
Consider the following argument:
'If a number is divisible by 6, then it is divisible by 3. The number n is not divisible by 3. Therefore, n is not divisible by 6.'

Which of the arguments below has the same logical structure as the argument above?

choices.A: If an animal is a mammal, then it has a four-chambered heart. This animal does not have a four-chambered heart. Therefore, this animal is not a mammal.
choices.B: If a student passed the course, then the student sat the final examination. This student did not pass the course. Therefore, this student did not sit the final examination.
choices.C: If it rains, the fixture is cancelled; and if the fixture is cancelled, the tickets are refunded. Therefore, if it rains, the tickets are refunded.
choices.D: If a compound is an alkali, then it turns red litmus paper blue. This compound is an alkali. Therefore, this compound turns red litmus paper blue.
choices.E: If a figure is a square, then it has four right angles. This figure has four right angles. Therefore, this figure is a square.

explanation: First strip the original to its form. With P = 'divisible by 6' and Q = 'divisible by 3', it reads: If P then Q; not Q; therefore not P. That is modus tollens — a valid form that works by denying the consequent. A parallel-reasoning question asks for the option with the identical abstract structure, regardless of subject matter. Testing each: B affirms the consequent (invalid), C denies the antecedent (invalid), D is modus ponens (valid but a different structure), and E is a two-step hypothetical syllogism. Only A — if P then Q; not Q; therefore not P — reproduces the exact form, so A is the match. The discipline is to compare logical skeletons, not topics or mere validity.

option_analysis.A: Correct: The original is modus tollens — If P then Q; not Q; therefore not P (P = 'divisible by 6', Q = 'divisible by 3'). This option has exactly that form: If P (mammal) then Q (four-chambered heart); not Q; therefore not P. Same valid structure, different content.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: This denies the antecedent — If P then Q; not P; therefore not Q — which is invalid (a student could sit the exam yet still fail). It negates the first part of the conditional, whereas modus tollens negates the consequent. Misconception: confusing denying the antecedent with denying the consequent.
option_analysis.C: Wrong: This is a hypothetical syllogism (a chain of two conditionals: If P then Q; if Q then R; therefore if P then R). It is valid but has three linked terms and no premise negating a component, so its structure differs from modus tollens. Misconception: treating any valid conditional argument as structurally identical.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: This is modus ponens — If P then Q; P; therefore Q — a valid form, but not the one in the original, which starts from the negation of the consequent rather than the affirmation of the antecedent. Misconception: matching only on validity while ignoring the specific structure.
option_analysis.E: Wrong: This affirms the consequent — If P then Q; Q; therefore P — an invalid form (a non-square rectangle also has four right angles). The original denies the consequent; this asserts it. Misconception: matching by surface topic or the mere presence of an 'if-then', while overlooking that this pattern is invalid.
